summary: Gives additional guidance on deploying NAT64 and 464XLAT in IPv6 networks, including cellular, broadband, and enterprise. It covers optimizations and issues for IPv6-only connectivity, such as DNS64, applications using literal IPv4 addresses, and IPv4-only hosts or applications.

plainLanguage.summary: Some websites still speak only the old internet language. This is advice for networks that must translate for them so everyone can still talk.

subtitle: Guidance for deploying NAT64 and 464XLAT in IPv6 networks.

tldr.problem: IPv6-only networks need to reach IPv4-only services and hosts, but NAT64 alone has limitations with DNSSEC, IPv4 literals, and IPv4-only hosts.
tldr.mechanism: NAT64 translates packets between IPv6 and IPv4; DNS64 synthesizes IPv6 addresses for IPv4 services; 464XLAT adds a customer-side translator (CLAT) on user devices to handle IPv4-only applications and improve DNSSEC handling.
tldr.outcome: Networks can provide IPv6-only access while maintaining compatibility with the IPv4 Internet, with trade-offs around DNSSEC, performance, and support for legacy applications.

today: RFC 8683 is an Informational RFC published in November 2019 and remains current guidance. NAT64/464XLAT is the predominant translation mechanism in cellular networks and is increasingly used in broadband deployments.

sections.title: IPv6-Only Connectivity and IPv4 Compatibility
sections.content:
NAT64 (RFC 6146) is a stateful IPv6-to-IPv4 translation mechanism that allows IPv6-only hosts to reach IPv4-only servers by translating packet headers. DNS64 (RFC 6147) synthesizes AAAA records from A records in DNS responses, so IPv6 applications can discover and reach IPv4 services by their domain names.

However, NAT64 and DNS64 have significant limitations: DNS64 modifies DNS answers, which can break DNSSEC validation; applications using literal IPv4 addresses or non-IPv6-compliant APIs bypass DNS64 and fail; IPv4-only hosts or applications behind an IPv6-only access link cannot use NAT64 at all. 464XLAT (RFC 6877) addresses these limitations by combining a customer-side translator (CLAT, a stateless NAT46) on user devices with the provider-side NAT64, allowing applications to use IPv4 even in IPv6-only networks.

This document provides deployment guidance for NAT64 and 464XLAT in cellular, broadband, and enterprise networks, examining different scenarios and the operational trade-offs of each approach.
sections.plainLanguage: Network translation lets IPv6-only networks talk to IPv4-only servers. The tricky parts are apps that don't use DNS, security checks that fail with modified DNS records, and devices that only speak IPv4. 464XLAT puts a translator on each device to handle those cases.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The document describes several deployment scenarios, grouped into categories: Known to Work scenarios are deployed in production by operators. These include: (1) Service Provider NAT64 with DNS64, the most common approach; (2) 464XLAT using DNS64, where the CLAT on user devices handles IPv4-only apps and the provider-side NAT64 and DNS64 handle the rest; (3) 464XLAT without DNS64, where CLAT handles all IPv4 traffic and DNSSEC is never broken because DNS64 doesn't modify records.

Known to Work under Special Conditions scenarios work only with significant caveats: NAT64 without DNS64 requires manual configuration or discovery mechanisms; NAT64 with DNS64 only in hosts requires all hosts to implement DNS64 locally; NAT64 with DNS64 only in the IPv4 remote network doesn't work for most cases because the remote side isn't deployed for IPv6.

Each scenario has different trade-offs regarding DNSSEC validity, support for IPv4 literals and non-IPv6 APIs, support for IPv4-only hosts, robustness to foreign DNS, DNS load optimization, and connection establishment delay optimization.
sections.plainLanguage: Different ways to set up the translation have different strengths. Some work great but might break security checks; some avoid security issues but add delay; some work only if everyone cooperates on DNS prefix configuration.

sections.title: Operational Issues and Solutions
sections.content:
Several issues require careful consideration when deploying NAT64/464XLAT: DNSSEC and DNS64 interact problematically because DNS64 modifies answers, triggering DNSSEC validation failures on validating resolvers. Solutions include having validators be DNS64-aware, not using DNS64 at all, or implementing CLAT with local DNS synthesis. IPv4 literals and non-IPv6-compliant APIs bypass DNS64; only CLAT or local address synthesis can handle these. IPv4-only hosts and applications behind an IPv6-only link need CLAT to function at all.

Foreign DNS (users switching to public DNS servers) can break deployments if the foreign DNS doesn't support DNS64 or uses a different prefix than the NAT64. CLAT mitigates most of these issues. Well-Known Prefix (WKP) vs. Network-Specific Prefix (NSP) for NAT64 is a configuration choice with implications for BGP routing and user flexibility. Explicit Address Mappings (EAM) allow CLAT to avoid double translation (NAT46 then NAT64) for known IPv6 destinations, improving performance.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS checks work better when the translator is DNS64-aware; old apps need a translator on the device; users changing their DNS setting shouldn't break things; you can optimize common paths so translation doesn't happen twice.

sections.title: 464XLAT Advantages
sections.content:
464XLAT provides a more complete solution because the CLAT on user devices handles IPv4-only applications and allows them to coexist with IPv6-native applications on the same device. When DNS64 is used with 464XLAT, IPv6 DNS queries go directly to NAT64 (one translation); IPv4 queries use CLAT then NAT64 (two translations) or are handled by EAM. When DNS64 is not used, all IPv4 traffic uses CLAT and NAT64, avoiding DNSSEC issues but adding modest overhead.

464XLAT is the only solution that fully supports IPv4-only hosts and applications behind an IPv6-only access link. It is standard in cellular networks, supporting scenarios like device tethering (sharing the cellular connection with other devices that may be IPv4-only). For broadband networks, 464XLAT on the customer edge router provides similar benefits. A DNS proxy at the CLAT can optimize DNS load by filtering out unnecessary queries.
sections.plainLanguage: 464XLAT puts a translator on each device, so old IPv4 apps work fine, and the device can simultaneously use the new IPv6 network. This is the only way to fully support devices that only speak IPv4.

sections.title: Enterprise and Broadband Deployment
sections.content:
NAT64/464XLAT deployment recommendations differ by network type. For Broadband managed networks where the provider controls the customer edge (CE) device, implementing 464XLAT with CLAT support is recommended to handle IPv4-only devices and applications. If the operator provides DNS, they should support DNS64 with DNSSEC-aware configuration, with additional safeguards like DNS proxy at the CE and ACLs for special cases.

For Cellular networks, 464XLAT is standard because devices often tether (share connectivity) to other devices that may be IPv4-only. UEs (User Equipment) typically use stateful NAT44 at the CLAT before the stateless NAT46 translation when a dedicated /64 isn't available. The operator should support DHCPv6-PD (prefix delegation) or similar to provide shorter prefixes so CEs can reserve a /64 for stateless NAT46.

Enterprise networks using IPv6-only access links can employ the same techniques. For example, an enterprise campus connecting to an IPv6-only ISP or using IPv6-only internal links can deploy NAT64 and 464XLAT similar to broadband deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: Broadband and enterprise networks should put a translator (CLAT) on the user device and let the network provide the big translator (NAT64). This way, old devices and apps just work, and modern devices also work well.
